title: Part 2: One lane per historian
text:
Last week the pipeline answered when Ashoka became a Buddhist. Six books, one paragraph, no sentence tied to a page.
The next question is shorter, and it is the one that breaks Phase 0.
How did he rule?
“He” is not a retrieval query. BM25 searches for the word. FAISS embeds a pronoun. Whatever comes back, the model fills in a king from pretraining, often the right one, for the wrong reason. Part 1 was the hybrid baseline. This post is Phase 1: the follow-up is rewritten before anything is searched, and two historians are held in separate lanes so they cannot be averaged.
The wiring is LangGraph. That is the least interesting sentence in this post.

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
section: What Phase 0 does with a follow-up
text:
What Phase 0 does with a follow-up
Phase 0 has no memory. Every question is the first question. “How did he rule his subjects?” is embedded as-is, mixed with whatever chunks sit near the word “he”, and written up as one voice. The chunk ids come afterwards, in a pile, which is what I showed last week.
A conversation with a book is mostly follow-ups. I keep a scripted one in the Phase 1 entrypoint, because a single polished query never shows this bug.

What did Guru Gobind Singh bring to Sikhi that was not there before?
How did he shape it according to the political conditions?
The militarisation of Sikhi, and his devotion to Shakti.
How did he meet Banda Singh Bahadur, and what did Banda do after his death?
Which battles did Banda fight, and how was he captured and killed?
The same capture, asked again, shorter.
What was his son’s name? Where was he from originally?
Then a hard cut. When did Ashoka become a Buddhist, before or after Kalinga, and why?
How did he take on the empire of his grandfather, and what did he add?
What did Ahilyabai Holkar actually do?
Which temples did she restore, and how, Somnath and Kashi?

Turns 2 to 7 are the same thread. “He” has to become Gobind Singh, and then, once Banda is the subject, Banda. Turn 7 is worse than a pronoun. Whose son? Turn 8 is a different century. If memory is doing its job, Ashoka is not answered out of the Sikh turns. Turn 9 is “he” again, and now “he” has to be Ashoka, not Banda. Turn 11 is “she”.
I am not pasting model answers for that conversation. A fluent paragraph hides the only line that matters. On each turn I print the rewritten question. If turn 9 still says Banda, the agent failed, whatever the prose looks like.

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
section: What Phase 1 does before it retrieves
text:
What Phase 1 does before it retrieves





flowchart TD
  Q["User question"] --> M["Memory<br/>pronoun, or similarity above 0.55"]
  M --> R["Small model rewrites<br/>last 3 turns only"]
  R --> P["Planner<br/>historians, sub-questions, lanes"]
  P --> L1["Lane: Romila Thapar"]
  P --> L2["Lane: R.K. Mukherjee"]
  L1 --> S["Synthesizer sees each lane<br/>under its own header"]
  L2 --> S
  S --> A["Answer<br/>inline chunk ids, then the dump"]






Two models. A small one, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, does the rewrite and the plan. The same 4-bit model as Phase 0 writes the answer. Planning is cheap and allowed to be wrong. The answer is the thing I do not want improvised.
Memory goes first. A question is a follow-up if it contains a pronoun, or if its embedding is close to the previous question, cosine above 0.55. The pronoun list is blunt: he, she, they, his, her, him, it, this, that, and a few cousins. If it is not a follow-up, I wipe the history. A new topic should not inherit the previous century. If it is a follow-up, I keep the last turns and append this question with an empty answer, which the synthesizer fills in later.
The rewrite uses that history and nothing else. The small model sees the last three turns. In the prompt, each previous answer is clipped to 200 characters. The instruction is narrow. If the question says he, she, they, it, or this, replace it with the person from the history. If the question already stands on its own, return it unchanged. Output only the question. If the result is shorter than a few characters, I throw it away and keep the original. I would rather search a pronoun than search a garbled sentence.
The planner turns one question into lanes. It has to return JSON: up to four historians, a sub-question for the work, whether a comparison was asked for, and one sentence on why. I parse it. If it is not JSON, the plan becomes a single lane called general and the rewritten question. The agent falls back toward Phase 0. It does not crash into a half-written plan.
Your names beat the planner. If you pass --historians, those labels are the lanes, and the model’s guess is ignored. That was deliberate. I do not want a 1.5B model deciding that “the nationalist view” is a person.
Lanes are zipped, one historian with one sub-question. If the planner wrote one sub-question and I asked for two historians, that question is copied into both lanes. The historians differ. The question does not. If the two lists disagree in length, both lanes get the rewritten question rather than a mismatched pair I cannot explain.





flowchart LR
  Q["How did Ashoka rule his subjects?"] --> O["Override beats the planner"]
  O --> A["lane_0 · Romila Thapar<br/>same question"]
  O --> B["lane_1 · R.K. Mukherjee<br/>same question"]
  A --> FA["Thapar's own FAISS<br/>or the global hybrid, if that index is missing"]
  B --> FB["Mukherjee's own FAISS<br/>or the global hybrid, if that index is missing"]
  FA --> H["Prompt, with a header per lane<br/>passage clipped to 300 characters"]
  FB --> H






Retrieval inside a lane is not the full Phase 0 stack, and I should say so.
If I can resolve the name to a per-historian FAISS index on disk, that lane searches only there. Names are normalised, then fuzzy-matched, SequenceMatcher at 0.75, so “RK Mukherjee” can still land on the Mukherjee bucket. I take that dense search and keep seven passages. There is no BM25 in that path, and no cross-encoder. I gave up the lexical channel on purpose. A nearer sentence from someone else must not be able to outrank Thapar inside Thapar’s lane.
If the folder is missing, the lane falls back to the Phase 0 hybrid retriever, BM25 plus FAISS plus the reranker, and I tag the metadata with the historian I asked for. The tag is not a wall. On a fresh clone, where index/ is gitignored and the per-historian folders were never built, both lanes search the same global pile. The header will still say Thapar. The passages might not.
The lanes run in parallel. Each one writes its own key into retrieved_results, and a dict merge keeps them from clobbering each other. Then a position object is built per lane: historian, passages, chunk ids.

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
section: What the synthesizer is allowed to see
text:
What the synthesizer is allowed to see
The evidence is not one bag. It is blocked.
--- LANE_0 ---
Historian: Romila Thapar

[chunk_id=EARLY_INDIA_RTH_...] first 300 characters of the passage

--- LANE_1 ---
Historian: R.K. Mukherjee

[chunk_id=ASOKA_RKM_...] first 300 characters of the passage
The outline above that evidence is a keyword switch, not a classifier. “Why” and “how did” get causes, evidence, interpretation. “Who” gets the person. “Compare” gets a comparison. Anything else gets a default of context, developments, evidence, significance. I would rather a slightly wrong heading than a model inventing its own structure and wandering off the pages.
The instruction is stricter than Phase 0, and also less honest about it. Phase 0 forbade the model from writing chunk ids, and I appended them myself. Phase 1 tells the model that every claim must cite [chunk_id=...], and then I still append up to twenty unique ids at the bottom. I do not trust the inline cites yet. The dump is the part I can check. The inline cite is the part I am trying to grow up into, which is Part 5, not this one.
Memory is updated from the answer, not from the whole answer. I store 400 characters. Past five turns, the older ones are summarised by the small model into a single note, and the recent five stay verbatim. The summary keeps names. It does not keep pages. That is good enough to resolve “she” to Ahilyabai. It is not good enough to cite her.
The command I actually want you to run:
python -m phase_1_agentic_rag.run_query \
  --query "How did Ashoka rule his subjects?" \
  --historians "Romila Thapar,R.K. Mukherjee" \
  --answer_style concise
Interactive, so you can ask “how did he rule?” as the second turn:
python -m phase_1_agentic_rag.run_query --interactive
There is a Gradio UI on --gradio. Same graph. The README in the Phase 1 folder still mentions an old module name, phase_1_newtesting. The command above is the one that exists.

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
section: The number I do not have
text:
The number I do not have
Phase 0 at least had a ROUGE, and I told you not to trust it. Phase 1’s --evaluate flag does not score anything. It runs that eleven-turn conversation and prints, for each turn, the rewritten question and the answer.
That is the right smoke test and a bad evaluation. I can see whether “he” survived. I cannot tell you whether Thapar’s lane stayed inside Thapar, or whether a cited chunk id actually contains the sentence. I am not going to invent a faithfulness number for a system I have not measured that way. The trace is the result. If the rewritten line is wrong, nothing downstream is worth reading.

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
text:
What I am not claiming
A lane is a wall between authors. It is not a historian, and it is not a graph.
“His son” is not clarified. It is guessed. The rewriter must return a question, not a question back. After a turn that mentions both Gobind Singh and Banda, “what was his son’s name?” will be resolved to somebody. A research assistant would ask which he. Mine picks. The pronoun list makes this worse in the other direction too. “This” and “that” count as follow-ups, so a fresh question that merely contains “that” inherits the previous person. And a real follow-up with no pronoun and different wording can fall under 0.55 and get its history wiped. Both errors are mine. The threshold is a constant I have not earned.
The comparison node is not doing the comparison. There is a claim aligner. It runs only if the planner sets use_claim_aligner. When it runs, it looks for structured claims on the lane. The position extractor never writes those claims. It writes passages. So the disagreement JSON is usually empty, and the thing that actually keeps the historians apart is the lane header in the prompt. I would rather show you that than pretend a node named “aligner” is reconciling Majumdar with Thapar.
Two passages count as enough. The evaluator replans if it sees fewer than two passages, and it will only do that once. Then it declares the evidence sufficient and synthesizes. Two chunks is a guard against an empty index. It is not a reading of the pages. Calling it an evaluator in a diagram is already more credit than the if statement deserves.
The model does not see the page. Each passage is clipped to 300 characters before synthesis. A qualification, a date, a “but his son”, often lives past character 300. Hybrid search can retrieve the right chunk and the prompt can still cut off the sentence that mattered. I have not fixed the clip.
A named lane drops BM25. Inside a historian index I search dense-only. Ashoka and Asoka are the sort of variation I built BM25 for in Phase 0, and the lane gives that up. The fallback, when the index folder is absent, gives up the wall instead. I do not currently have both.
None of this answers “did Savarkar’s writing reach Bhagat Singh?” A lane can hand me Thapar’s passages and Mukherjee’s passages. It still needs one chunk that happens to contain both people, or the model will build the edge itself. That edge is Part 3. People, organisations, a timeline, checked against the vector hits rather than hoped for inside a 1,600-character window.
Code: github.com/mekanavsharma/the-digital-historian

title: Part 2: One lane per historian
text:
Next Saturday
Part 3 is the same books, and a question a lane cannot represent. Who was associated with Abhinav Bharat, and which of those links is actually written down?
I want the relation to come from a graph I can open, not from a paragraph that sounds like it read one. If the graph and the pages disagree, the pages win. That rule is the whole post.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
text:
Last weekPhase 1 a lane could keep Romila Thapar out of R.K. Mukherjee’s paragraph. It still could not answer who was associated with Abhinav Bharat, unless some 1,600-character window happened to contain both names.
A relation is not a nearest neighbour. It is an edge. I said the edge had to come from a graph I can open, and that if the graph and the pages disagreed, the pages would win.
I built the graph. Then I ran the question. The pages do not win. On the default path, the question never reaches the graph at all.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
section: What a bag of chunks does with a membership
text:
What a bag of chunks does with a membership
“Who was associated with Abhinav Bharat?” is two entities and a predicate. Phase 0 embeds the whole sentence and hopes a chunk holds the predicate. Phase 1 can put Thapar in one lane and Majumdar in another, and still hope. Hope is how a model invents a member list that sounds like a book.
Phase 2 is the attempt to stop hoping. spaCy reads the corpus. A verb I recognise becomes an edge. The edge goes into Neo4j. A year, when I can see one, goes into SQLite. A question is then sent to the graph, the timeline, the Phase 0 hybrid retriever, or all three. The answer is still written by the same Phase 0 prompt. The graph does not get its own voice. It has to show up as evidence, or it does not count.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
section: The router is a pile of phrases, and this question misses it
text:
The router is a pile of phrases, and this question misses it
There is no model in the router. I score the question with lists.
Relationship phrases, “who fought whom”, “allied with”, “succeeded by”, “ruled by”, add 2 to graph. Time phrases, “before”, “after”, “when”, “year”, add 1 to timeline. Comparison phrases, “compare”, “according to”, “cross-check”, or the names Majumdar and Sarkar, add 2 to verification. A question of eight words or fewer adds 1 to vector, which is the Phase 0 retriever. The biggest score wins. The confidence I store next to that choice, 0.92 or 0.88 or 0.78, is a number I typed. It is not a probability.





flowchart TD
  Q["Question"] --> R["Phrase scores<br/>not a model"]
  R --> G["Graph<br/>1-hop around a capitalised name"]
  R --> T["Timeline<br/>SQLite, years 1000 to 2029"]
  R --> V["Vector<br/>Phase 0 hybrid, then keep 5"]
  R --> X["Verification<br/>graph, then pages, then years"]
  G --> E{"Any edges?"}
  E -->|no| V
  E -->|yes| S["Same Phase 0 prompt"]
  T --> S
  V --> S
  X --> S






Now the question I have been pointing at for two weeks.
Who were associated with Abhinav Bharat?
Six words. “Associated” is not in the relationship list. “Fought”, “allied”, “succeeded”, and “ruled” are. So graph stays at 0. Vector gets 1 for being short. The router calls it a fact lookup and sends it to hybrid search. The README has a second command, --retrieval-mode graph, because the first command does not do what the heading says. I am glad that second command is there. I am not going to describe the first one as graph retrieval.
“Who fought whom in 1526?” does hit the list. “Who fought whom” is worth 2, and that beats the short-question point for vector. The router is right. The retriever then looks for a capitalised name to center the subgraph on. “Who” is a stop word. 1526 is not a name. The entity list is empty. An empty list matches nothing. Auto mode sees no edges and falls back to the same hybrid search Phase 0 would have run. A forced graph mode does not fall back. It says the relationship was never extracted, which is the more honest failure, and also not an answer.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
text:
What actually gets written down
Ingest is where the graph is decided. I do not ask a model to invent triples. en_core_web_sm reads each sentence. If the verb’s lemma is in a map, the subject and object become an edge, and only if both look like proper names. “Defeated” becomes FOUGHT_AGAINST. “Founded” becomes FOUNDED. “Associated” becomes ASSOCIATED_WITH. If the parse finds nothing, a few regular expressions run, including “was a member of” and “associated with”. If those find nothing either, and the sentence contains a person and an organisation, every person is tied to every organisation with ASSOCIATED_WITH.
That last rule is how a membership question gets answers, and how it gets false ones. Coincidence and membership are the same edge. The lemma map has the same disease one level up. “Follow” is coded as succession. A sentence about a courtier who followed Akbar to a campaign can become SUCCEEDED_BY. I would rather miss that edge than crown the courtier. I have not taught the map the difference.
Two choices in the ingest matter more than the schema poster.
I extract per page, not per chunk, when you pass --page-mode. The pieces of HCIP_RCM_V2_C5_P143_0 and _1 are put back into one page before spaCy sees them. A relation that I split at 1,600 characters can be a sentence again. The id stored on the edge is the page id, with the piece number stripped.
And the only years I keep are 1000 to 2029. A four-digit year in that range becomes a Year node, and a battle or a treaty on that page is linked to it with OCCURRED_IN. 265 BCE does not match the pattern. The Kalinga question from Part 1 cannot become a timeline, because the timeline does not believe in dates before 1000. Ancient history, in this store, is a string.
The edges carry the sentence. At ingest I write context, the chunk id, and the page onto the relationship. That was the whole point. An edge you cannot open back onto a page is a rumour.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
section: What the query path does with it
text:
What the query path does with it





flowchart LR
  N["Capitalised name"] --> C["Neo4j: name CONTAINS that string<br/>1 hop, undirected, no year filter"]
  C --> F["Drop relation types I did not allow"]
  F --> P["Prompt line:<br/>Person:X --ASSOCIATED_WITH--> Organization:Y"]
  P --> L["Phase 0 generator<br/>cites graph-1 if the page id was not read back"]






The query path does not run the Cypher I was most careful about. I wrote a query that puts WHERE before OPTIONAL MATCH, because in Neo4j a WHERE after OPTIONAL MATCH filters the optional part and lets the main match return everything. That query is in the file. graph_search does not call it. It asks for a one-hop subgraph around the name, undirected, CONTAINS rather than an exact name, and then filters relation types in Python. The Cypher printed in the log is a comment that says no traversal query was used. I am not going to pretend the database did a join I didn’t send.
CONTAINS is a blunt instrument. “Ali” sits inside longer names. One hop is also blunt, in the other direction. Savarkar to a society to a second person is two hops. I clamp the walk at one. The chain I said I wanted is not the chain I retrieve.
The year is parsed and then dropped. “1526” is pulled out with the same 1000-to-2029 expression. The subgraph query does not receive it. The rows that come back do not include relationship properties, so the Python year check has nothing to compare. Who fought whom in 1526 is not a question about 1526. It is a question about whoever was capitalised, and in that particular wording, nobody was.
Worse, the sentence I stored is not read back. The return clause asks for the two names and the type of the edge. It does not ask for context, the chunk id, or the page. The prompt therefore sees a line like:
Graph evidence: Person:Vinayak Savarkar --ASSOCIATED_WITH--> Organization:Abhinav Bharat
No page. The citation helper, finding no chunk id, writes graph-1. That is not a page in any book I own. The justification is sitting on the relationship in Neo4j. The answer path forgot to pick it up.
If auto mode finds no edges, it calls the Phase 0 retriever, and those passages do have real chunk ids. A forced --retrieval-mode graph will not make that call. Empty stays empty. I prefer the forced mode when I am testing the graph, because the fallback hides it.
A timeline question with a four-digit year is a real range query, year BETWEEN, ordered by year, twenty rows. A timeline question without one, which is every ancient question, searches the first capitalised name with LIKE. “Before and after Kalinga” is that search. Kalinga may be in the table. 265 is not.
Verification, the fourth door, runs all three and then compares them. Agreement is true if any graph name appears inside a retrieved passage, or if the timeline returned any year at all. A year with no shared entity still counts. Nothing is deleted when agreement is false. The verdict is written into the prompt as one more passage: “Agreement=true” or not. The page cannot strike an edge. Last week’s rule is not in this code. An empty graph loses to the pages. A wrong graph is shown beside them.
The generator is unchanged. build_prompt from Phase 0, the same 4-bit model, the same instruction to stay inside the context, the same chunk ids appended afterwards. On a graph hit, part of that context is the triple, not the book. The model will recite the triple. I told it the triple was evidence.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
text:
What I am not claiming
I am not claiming a knowledge graph of Indian history. I am claiming a heuristic one, and the heuristics have a shape I can list.
The question I care about does not route. “Associated with” is the relation I extract and the phrase I forgot to score. Until I add it, Abhinav Bharat is a vector query, unless I force the mode.
The graph is case-sensitive in the only way that hurts. Entities are capitalised spans. The README’s own example, “Abhinava bharat”, keeps “Abhinava” and drops “bharat”. A lower-case name is not in the graph lookup, even if the edge exists.
BCE is out of range. The timeline is a modern-year index with a keyword fallback. It will not order Ashoka, the Kalinga war, and the edicts. Part 1’s question is still a vector question, and it should be.
One hop, no sentence. The walk stops at the first neighbour, and the neighbour arrives without the sentence or the page. graph-1 is a confession, not a citation.
“Follow” is not always a succession, and a shared sentence is not always a membership. Both of those edges will look identical to the true ones in the prompt. I have no count of how often. Phase 2 has no evaluation flag that scores an edge against the sentence it came from. I am not going to invent a precision number for a triple store I have not audited.
The pages do not win a disagreement. They win an absence. That is a fallback, not a rule.
What I will claim is smaller. The hybrid retriever is still the retriever. The graph is a second index, built from verbs and names, stored so a relationship can be listed without rereading the book. Page-level ingest is the right cut, because the chunk boundary was the original bug. And a triple that cannot show its sentence is not yet a source.
python -m phase_2_graph_rag.run_query --ingest --reset --page-mode

python -m phase_2_graph_rag.run_query \
  --query "Who were associated with Abhinav Bharat?"

python -m phase_2_graph_rag.run_query \
  --query "Who were associated with Abhinav Bharat?" \
  --retrieval-mode graph

python -m phase_2_graph_rag.run_query --visualize "Akbar"
The visualization is an HTML file from PyVis, under phase_2_graph_rag/artifacts/visualizations/. The Phase 2 README still says PNG. The file you can open is the HTML. Neo4j has to be up. The query command does not quietly switch to the in-memory graph. Set NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USER, NEO4J_PASSWORD, and NEO4J_DATABASE yourself.
Code: github.com/mekanavsharma/the-digital-historian

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
text:
Next Saturday
The labels have been on the chunks since the data prep. Ancient or medieval or modern. Nationalist, Marxist, or neither. Phase 2’s verifier never reads them. It looks for a shared string.
Part 4 is that shelf. A question goes to a period and a school before retrieval, the other passages are dropped, and the model is trained to answer from the pages it was given and ignore the ones that were only nearby. An edge without a sentence is a problem. A paragraph that blends three schools of history is the older one, and it is still open.

title: Part 3: History is a graph, not a bag of chunks
section: The problem: questions chunks can’t answer
text:
The problem: questions chunks can’t answer
Look at this query from my own test list:

“Who were associated with Abhinav Bharat?”

A chunk-based pipeline, however good, has a hard time with it. The answer isn’t in one paragraph. It is scattered across many chunks, in different chapters and books, each mentioning one or two names. To answer well, the system has to collect those mentions and connect them.
There is a whole family of questions like this:

Association: who worked with whom, who belonged to which organisation.
Chronology: what happened before or after an event, and in what order.
Aggregation: list everything connected to a person, place or movement.
Reconciliation: two books give different dates, and which one do the other sources support?

Top-k text retrieval returns the most similar passages. These questions need the connections between passages. That is what a graph stores.
